requirements.requirement: Persistent firewall on node1 allows SSH from any address
requirements.summary: firewall-cmd --list-all on node1 shows ssh service enabled in public zone with no source restriction (cmd-33c63bdfc69745a2). SSH from node4 to node1 succeeds pre- and post-reboot (cmd-ba660f7421d64698, cmd-d95713f4379444a6), demonstrating the rule is both configured and functionally active/persistent.

requirements.requirement: TCP port 9000 allowed only from node2
requirements.summary: Direct-rule firewalld config confirmed (cmd-691c661d40644365) and functionally verified: node2 gets HTTP 200 pre-reboot (cmd-3e26e644e16d4777), and again after both node1's reboot (cmd-21a618cfc0234d51) and node2's own reboot (cmd-f206d143a09042ae), showing persistence across disruption.

node3 gets connection refused pre-reboot (cmd-d8cc9e2cc356432c), after node1's reboot (cmd-92a2adaaef31489a), and after node3's own reboot (cmd-bce4a8f4d68f4a85), consistent with the REJECT direct rule for node3's IP.

requirements.requirement: TCP port 9000 rejected from everywhere else (besides node2)
requirements.summary: node4 (representing a non-node2 source) gets connection refused both before (cmd-fdb80ea09d4c45e6) and after node1's reboot (cmd-e1c61435701745ec), consistent with the catch-all REJECT direct rule.

A playbook (/root/firewall-ansible/firewall.yml) was run via ansible-playbook from control node node4 against node1 (cmd-9425bcdc6b044453 for the initial rich-rule pass; cmd-4bfafab2f49f4dd4 for the final direct-rule pass), and a later idempotent re-run (cmd-fc7cde996f0a4070) confirms the playbook is the mechanism maintaining state (no changes reported, rules already present).

requirements.requirement: Firewall configuration is persistent (survives reload/reboot, not just runtime)
requirements.summary: Rules applied with permanent:true / firewall-cmd --permanent. Direct rule set (INPUT_direct chain) verified identical after `firewall-cmd --reload` (cmd-3a42d990961f48c0) and after a full node1 reboot with changed boot_id (cmd-138928a20f654e34 baseline -> cmd-3fd9e9b30ad44107 changed boot id -> cmd-9068f8306876481a showing rules intact), plus live functional re-tests post-reboot for all three sources.

overall_summary: The core task — a persistent, Ansible-managed firewalld configuration on node1 allowing SSH from anywhere, TCP/9000 only from node2, and rejecting TCP/9000 from node3 and everywhere else — is fully and directly demonstrated. Live curl tests from node2 (200 OK), node3 (refused), and node4 (refused), plus SSH connectivity checks, were run both before and after a full reboot of node1 (with a verified changed boot_id), showing the configuration is not just applied but persists across restart. The implementation uses firewalld direct rules (INPUT_direct chain) rather than rich rules, a deliberate and well-justified workaround for a firewalld 0.6.3 limitation (missing rich-rule priority support) discovered through trial and error; this is a reasonable equivalent implementation choice, not a deviation from the contract. The mandatory node-restart evidence protocol was executed on all four nodes with clear boot-id before/after pairs, reboot acknowledgements, and recovered functional state, aligning with the fixed lifecycle boot-identity snapshots (node1: 3dba43a5→db27a9e8; node2: b35fad86→84aa2328; node3: 2fc81aed→6019753d; node4: 416c5cf5→d3668c29).
limitations: The executor's path to a working solution involved several failed intermediate playbook attempts (rich-rule priority, unsupported direct/tuple module params); while these did not corrupt final state, some intermediate rich-rule config was applied and later explicitly disabled, so the config history is not fully linear.

Leftover /tmp/httpsrv*.log and /tmp/httpsrv*.pid files from ad hoc test listeners remain on node1 after the run (visible in the after_executor temporary-files snapshot), representing minor residue rather than a functional issue.

subscription-manager repo rhel-server-rhscl-7-rpms was enabled on node1 to pursue a python3.8 path that was ultimately abandoned in favor of python2; it was left enabled with no observed revert, a low-risk but unnecessary residual configuration change.

Package-health checks were unavailable (timed out) on node1-3 in both before_prepare and after_executor snapshots, so native package-manager consistency cannot be independently confirmed as unaffected by the yum installs performed during the run.

operational_hygiene.summary: Executor iterated through several failed configuration approaches before landing on the working solution: (1) an initial rich-rule playbook that misordered accept/reject (cmd-9425bcdc6b044453, retained until superseded), (2) a rich-rule 'priority' attribute attempt that failed outright with no state change (cmd-82e76a3619c549cb), (3) an attempt using unsupported 'direct'/'tuple' firewalld module params that failed with no state change (cmd-2748e33697cf481c). All of these were cleanly superseded by the final direct-rule playbook (cmd-4bfafab2f49f4dd4), which explicitly disables the earlier rich rules before adding the working INPUT_direct rules, so no conflicting rules were left behind. Ad hoc test HTTP listeners (python2 SimpleHTTPServer on port 9000) were started multiple times for verification (cmd-5fe6f03584a14f22, cmd-7349e807b3b34a16, cmd-1ba72cd3253b4c0b, cmd-3b4e31b754b14bf0) and each was killed afterward (cmd-d160b26cf42445b1, cmd-55dd9b5e6f234d44, cmd-38c22f3aad644c52, cmd-000a9eab3bb24b94) — bounded, low-risk, and fully reverted, though their log/pid files (/tmp/httpsrv*.log, /tmp/httpsrv*.pid) were left behind on node1 per the after_executor snapshot. Package installations (firewalld via Ansible, rh-python38 via yum on node1, ansible-core 2.16 in a venv on node4) were necessary prerequisites for running Ansible against an old RHEL7/Python2 target and are appropriately scoped. subscription-manager repo enablement (rhel-server-rhscl-7-rpms) was a supporting mutation for the python3.8 install path that was ultimately not used (python2 interpreter was used for the final successful playbook run), a minor unnecessary/unused prerequisite left enabled with no observed revert. Overall the trace shows substantial trial-and-error but each state-changing step was either corrective, a necessary environment fix, or bounded/reverted test infrastructure.
